name: Uma Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I sell new-build homes for the new homes team at Ashby Residential, an agency that handles sales for developers. Right now I'm based in the show home at Orchard Rise, a site of a hundred and forty houses on the edge of the city. My day is walking people through the show home, talking them through floor plans and parking, then chasing mortgage offers and reservation forms. I like the pace and the targets. I don't like the days when the site's mud up to your ankles and nobody turns up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use it to write follow-up emails after each visit, to compare which plots are selling, and to prep answers before a buyer meeting. I set up a little system that tells me who's gone quiet after a viewing. I'm about average at the actual selling, but I'm quick, and I like trying new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool, not a miracle, and that's fine. At work I'd keep using what works. Online I'd post a few tips for other agents, because people always ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. My job is steady, and I'm a bit ahead of the people who never bothered with the tools. My savings are good and I've got the studio flat I rent out, so money isn't a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling at Orchard Rise and move to the next site when it finishes. I'd keep my AI follow-up system and share it with the team. I'd probably look for a second small flat to buy in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite happy, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the studio flat.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought it two years ago with money my gran left me plus my own savings. It's a studio near the hospital, and a junior doctor rents it. The rent covers the mortgage and a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New-build sales go up and down with interest rates and how many houses developers start. If a developer pauses a site, our team gets moved around or cut. That's always there, AI or not.

With savings and **the studio flat**, money isn't a worry.

Look for **a second flat** in the next couple of years.

fieldNote: Her one standing risk is **developers pausing** sites.

steps.text: Share her AI follow-up system with the new homes team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and people who learn now will be fine. At work I'd offer to train the team. To friends I'd say it's a good time to be good with this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a good spot. The email, booking and follow-up side is already mostly done by my tools, and a show home still needs someone in it. The risk is that each site needs one person instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ashby to let me run the AI setup for all the new homes sites, not just mine. I'd try to get a bonus or a title for it, like sales systems lead. And I'd keep saving for the second flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited. It's the version where being early pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would lose out in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Gemma, who's lovely but hates computers and does everything on paper. If a site goes from two of us to one, it'll be the one with the tools who stays. I'd try to help her, but she has to want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If every site needs fewer people, there are fewer jobs for me to move to later. It's a smaller industry. I'd just need to be one of the people left.

I'd tell friends it's a **good time** to be good with tools.
think: I'm in **a good spot**, already doing the follow-up work with tools.
Each site might need **one person** instead of two.
do: Ask to run the **AI setup** for every new homes site.
Push for a **systems lead** title or bonus.
S1.quote: If a site goes from two of us to one, it'll be the one with the tools who stays.
fieldNote: She expects to **gain** from being early.

steps.text: Offer to run the AI follow-up setup across all new homes sites
Ask Ashby for a sales systems lead title and bonus
Keep saving for a deposit on a second flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and people need help, and quickly. At work I'd be very practical: here's what we keep, here's what we change. Online I'd probably share what I'm doing, because people would be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the agency side of new-build sales almost disappears. Developers would sell straight through AI, with one person on site to open the show home. I think I could be that person, or the one managing several sites' systems, but it's a much smaller job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd talk to the developer at Orchard Rise, not just Ashby, because they're who'll still be hiring. I'd offer to run their sales system across sites. In the first year I'd also buy the second flat if prices dip, because rent is the income I trust most when jobs wobble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. I've got the studio, the savings and the skills. I'd just feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is part show home, part screen. Does the three years before robots matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Opening the show home, walking people round, handing over keys, that stays human until about 2031. I don't think a buyer spends three hundred thousand without a person in the room yet. That buys me a few years to shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about people renting your flats if lots of jobs go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the scary bit, honestly. If the junior doctor loses work, or rents fall, my plan wobbles. Doctors seem safer than most, so I'd keep it.

I'd share online **what I'm doing** to calm others.
think: The **agency side** of new-build sales almost disappears.
I could be the **one person** on site, but it's a smaller job.
do: Approach **the Orchard Rise developer** directly to run its sales system across sites.
Buy **a second flat** in the first year if prices dip.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, with the **ground moving**, but not scared.

fieldNote: She plans to **jump to the developer**, skipping the agency.
She admits her plan wobbles if **tenants lose work**.

steps.text: Pitch the Orchard Rise developer on running its AI sales across sites

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start. At work I'd lead on the changeover. To friends I'd say this is the time to build something of your own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty calm. Five years is time to become the person developers call. And with robots another three years behind, the show home part lasts until around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd set up a small side business advising developers on AI sales systems, evenings and weekends. I'd buy the second flat. And I'd keep selling at Ashby while it's paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave Ashby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably by year three, if the side business takes off. I'd give them proper notice. I'm not trying to burn bridges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the side business fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the side business fails, I've learned a lot and I've still got the flats and savings. I'd go back to selling for a developer. I think the downside's small.

I'd tell friends it's time to **build something** of their own.
think: I'd be **pretty calm** with time to become the person developers call.
The **show home** part lasts until around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous and everyone should use it. At work I'd say let's be first, not last. To friends I'd say learn the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be 37 when it arrives. I'd have years to build up the flats and the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling and push for team lead in the next two years. I'd buy another flat every few years if the numbers work. I'd build the AI sales service slowly, and go full time on it only when I had enough clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Maybe a bit too relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Too relaxed how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years can make you lazy. I've watched people at work put off learning anything new because there's always next year. I'd set myself checkpoints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a checkpoint be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every year, I'd check how many staff each site needs. If it drops from two to one, I move faster. If not, I keep going as I am.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even with a plan it would be a scramble, and my tenants might lose work too. What would help is clear rules on how fast firms can cut staff, and short business courses for people starting something new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe people like me make things worse by helping firms need fewer staff. I'd still do it, because someone will. I think about that sometimes.

headlineQuote: Maybe people like me make things worse by helping firms need fewer staff. I'd still do it, because someone will.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old new-build sales negotiator** working from show homes for an agency's new homes team.
She uses **AI tools every day** and built her own follow-up system.
She owns **a rental studio** and plans to buy more flats.
She stays **calm** or **uneasy** across all scenarios, planning to move to developers or start a side business.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028**, which would mean a scramble and possible tenant job losses.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **rules** on how fast firms cut staff, and short **business courses**.
